title: 1.3 Core Calculations
summary: You do not need advanced mathematics to start learning trading.
bodyHtml:
1.3 Core Calculations

Why This Matters

You do not need advanced mathematics to start learning trading.

You do need reliable basic math.

Before you place any trade, you should be able to answer one question:

If this idea is wrong, how much money can I lose?

This lesson shows the small amount of math needed to answer that question.

What You Should Understand After This Lesson

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

  • calculate simple trade risk using a stop distance, a unit value, and a size;
  • explain why the same-looking move can mean different money in different products;
  • avoid the most common beginner unit mistakes.

The Core Formula

The basic formula is:

cash risk = distance to stop x value of one movement unit x quantity

Now turn that into plain language:

  • distance to stop = how far your stop loss is from your entry;
  • value of one movement unit = how much one pip, tick, point, or dollar move is worth;
  • quantity = how many shares, contracts, or lots you are trading.

That is the foundation of beginner trade math.

Step 1: Measure the Distance

If you enter at one price and your stop is lower or higher, the gap between them is your stop distance.

Examples:

  • A stock trade with a stop $2 away has a distance of $2.
  • An FX trade with a stop 20 pips away has a distance of 20 pips.
  • A futures trade with a stop 10 ticks away has a distance of 10 ticks.

The number is useless until you also know the unit.

Step 2: Know the Value of One Unit

This is where many beginners go wrong.

The same-looking move can mean very different money:

  • 1 share moving by $1 is usually worth $1 per share;
  • 1 tick in an E-mini S&P 500 future is worth $12.50 per contract;
  • 1 tick in NYMEX WTI crude oil is worth $10 per contract.

The market does not care what feels small on the chart. The contract rules decide what the move is worth.

Step 3: Multiply by Your Size

Once you know the distance and the value of one unit, multiply by the size you plan to trade.

That turns a chart idea into a money amount.

Worked Example 1: Shares

Imagine:

  • you buy 50 shares;
  • your stop is $2 away;
  • each $1 move in one share is worth $1.

So:

cash risk = 2 x 1 x 50 = $100

If the stop is hit, the planned loss is about $100.

Worked Example 2: FX

Imagine:

  • your stop is 20 pips away;
  • your platform shows that each pip is worth $5 at your chosen size;
  • your quantity is already built into that $5 pip value.

So:

cash risk = 20 x 5 = $100

This is why traders must check pip value before pressing the button.

Worked Example 3: Futures

CME explains that:

  • one E-mini S&P 500 tick is worth $12.50;
  • one NYMEX WTI crude oil tick is worth $10.

If your WTI stop is 10 ticks away and you trade 1 contract:

cash risk = 10 x 10 x 1 = $100

If your E-mini S&P 500 stop is 10 ticks away and you trade 1 contract:

cash risk = 10 x 12.50 x 1 = $125

Same number of ticks. Different money.

Same Number, Different Risk

Trade example Distance Unit value Quantity Total risk
Shares $2 $1 per share 50 shares $100
FX 20 pips $5 per pip included in pip value $100
WTI futures 10 ticks $10 per tick 1 contract $100
E-mini S&P futures 10 ticks $12.50 per tick 1 contract $125

(Table alt-text: A beginner trade-risk table comparing shares, FX, WTI futures, and E-mini S&P futures, showing how distance, unit value, and quantity combine to create total cash risk.)

Notional Value: A Different Calculation

Sometimes you also need to know the full size of the position, not just the planned loss.

That is called notional value.

The simple formula is:

notional value = price x quantity

Example:

  • 100 shares of a stock priced at $50
  • notional value = 50 x 100 = $5,000

Notional value is not the same as cash risk.

  • Notional value tells you the full size of the position.
  • Cash risk tells you how much you plan to lose if the stop is hit.

You need both ideas, but you must not confuse them.

Common Beginner Mistakes

Mistake 1: Choosing Size First

The correct order is:

  1. find the stop distance;
  2. check the unit value;
  3. calculate the size.

Not the other way around.

Mistake 2: Mixing Ticks, Pips, and Points

If you use the wrong unit, your risk number becomes wrong immediately.

Mistake 3: Thinking the Same Chart Shape Means the Same Risk

A setup that looks “small” on one product can still be expensive on another product.

Mistake 4: Confusing Notional Value With Planned Loss

A big notional value does not automatically mean a big loss. A small notional value does not automatically mean a safe trade. Stop distance and unit value still matter.
learningOutcomes: calculate simple price-distance and cash-risk examples across more than one asset class;
explain why the same move size does not create the same dollar impact in every product;
avoid the most common unit mistakes before they reach the order screen.

quizItems.prompt: What must you know before you can convert a stop distance into cash risk?

choices.label: B
choices.text: The value of one unit of movement and the quantity traded

correctAnswer.label: B
correctAnswer.text: The value of one unit of movement and the quantity traded

quizItems.explanation: Stop distance alone is not enough. You must know the cash value of that movement for the chosen size.

quizItems.prompt: Why can two 20-unit moves create very different cash results?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Because every product uses the same contract size

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because movement units and contract values differ across products

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because all markets settle in the same currency

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because volatility removes the need for sizing

correctAnswer.label: B
correctAnswer.text: Because movement units and contract values differ across products

quizItems.explanation: A 20-pip FX move and a 20-tick futures move can represent very different cash effects.

quizItems.prompt: Which sequence is most disciplined for a beginner?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Choose the size first, then estimate risk

choices.label: B
choices.text: Choose the market first, then ignore unit value

choices.label: C
choices.text: Measure stop distance, confirm unit value, then determine size

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pick leverage, then look for a chart

correctAnswer.label: C
correctAnswer.text: Measure stop distance, confirm unit value, then determine size

quizItems.explanation: Risk should be translated from the plan into size, not guessed after the trade is chosen.
